## Micah 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview / Structure

The chapter is a "covenant lawsuit" (a *rîb* or legal controversy) in which God brings His case against Israel in a cosmic courtroom, with the mountains and hills summoned as witnesses. It moves between three speakers: the LORD as plaintiff, the people (or a representative voice) responding, and the prophet as God's attorney. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)

**Walter Kaiser's Outline** (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary):
- Have I Mistreated You? (vv. 1–3)
- Have I Required Too Much From You? (vv. 4–8)
- Have I Approved of Your Exploiting One Another? (vv. 9–12)
- Have I Blessed Your Get-Rich-Quick Schemes? (vv. 13–16)

---

### v. 1 — "Hear now what the LORD says: 'Arise, plead your case before the mountains...'"

- **Courtroom scene**: Micah pictures a court of law. God commands the prophet to "Arise" (stand up — court is in session) and "plead your case before the mountains." The mountains and hills serve as the jury, having been present when Yahweh ratified His covenant with His people. They are "unshakable witnesses." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)
- **Ellicott**: The third portion of Micah's prophecy opens with "a solemn appeal to Nature to hear the Lord pleading with His people," similar to Deuteronomy 32:1: "Give ear, O ye heavens, and hear, O earth." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill**: The Lord commands Micah to "contend" before the mountains. The mountains and hills — clothed with grass, flocks, and fruit trees — had witnessed both God's goodness and Israel's idolatry upon every high hill. Some Jewish interpreters (Kimchi, Ben Melech) understood "mountains" as the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) and "hills" as the matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah) called as witnesses from their graves. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)
- **Precept Austin** (NET note): "As in some ancient Near Eastern treaties, the mountains are personified as legal witnesses that will settle the dispute between God and Israel." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)

---

### v. 2 — "Hear, O mountains, the LORD's indictment, you enduring foundations of the earth..."

- **Guzik**: God brings His "complaint" (legal case) against His people. He will "contend" with Israel. The mountains are called "strong foundations of the earth" — enduring, unchanging witnesses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Gill**: The "strong foundations of the earth" refers to the mountains as the strong parts of the earth, the bottoms of them being the foundations. Dreadful when God brings a charge and pleads His own cause against sinful men. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: The Mosaic covenant was cut at Mount Sinai; the written tablets were placed in the Ark as "a witness against you" (Deut 31:26). The mountains therefore stand as witnesses to the very covenant Israel has broken. Yahweh is both Plaintiff and Judge; later He will also act as prosecuting attorney (vv. 6–12) and pass sentence (vv. 13–16). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)

---

### v. 3 — "'My people, what have I done to you? Testify against Me how I have wearied you!'"

- **Guzik**: God asks a stunning question: "What have I done to you?" He had done nothing but good; Israel repaid Him with rebellion. The question is rhetorical — they have no answer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Gill**: "What iniquity have you or your fathers found in Me?" God condescends to have the case fairly debated. He asks: what heavy yoke, what grievous commandments, what burdensome sacrifices? All He had promised He had performed. "Astonishing condescension and goodness!" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: God still calls them "My people" despite their rebellion — a testimony to His steadfast covenant loyalty. Butler notes that God invites Israel to declare His "faults" which would justify their departure from Him — but they have none. Kaiser sees this as God turning the tables: rather than charging them directly, He asks whether they have any charge against Him. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)
- **Spurgeon** (quoted on Precept Austin): "What but good, what but mercy, have I done unto thee?" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)

---

### v. 4 — "For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: God rehearses His saving acts: redemption from Egypt, and the gift of godly leaders. This is His case for the defence — He has done them only good. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: Israel remains silent after the rhetorical question, so the Lord continues to plead: "I showed thee the greatest mercies: I redeemed thee out of Egypt, the house of bondage." Moses, Aaron, and Miriam are noted as the three great members of the family commissioned to carry out the Divine decree. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill**: Instead of doing them wrong, God did them great good. The redemption was "out of the house of servants" — some rabbis took this as meaning the Egyptians themselves were "servants of servants" (descendants of Ham under Noah's curse), making Israel's redemption from them an even greater blessing. Moses taught the judgments, Aaron made atonement, and Miriam instructed the women (per the Targum). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "My people, remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered. Remember your journey from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: Balak and Balaam (Numbers 22–24) illustrate that God could never be persuaded to curse Israel. Balaam blessed Israel four times. However, Balaam then counseled Balak to lead Israel into fornication and idolatry — and Israel *did* bring a curse on themselves through their own sin (24,000 died by plague). The point: if Israel felt cursed, it was entirely their own doing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: This is a "signal instance of the controlling power of God." Balaam was constrained to bless when he had the highest motive to curse — "the most conclusive instance extant of the will of man controlled to do the exact opposite of his intended action." "Righteousness" here means rather "liberality, beneficence" — God's faithful covenant kindness. The journey "from Shittim to Gilgal" refers to the miraculous Jordan crossing and the covenant renewal at Gilgal (Joshua 4). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill**: Balak consulted Balaam "from place to place" trying to get the God of Israel to turn against His people. The phrase "from Shittim unto Gilgal" may be proverbial ("from place to place"). Gill notes that at Shittim Israel sinned and yet God spared a remnant; at Gilgal the covenant of circumcision was renewed and the first Passover in the land was kept — both evidence of God's faithfulness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

---

### vv. 6–7 — "With what shall I come before the LORD... Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression?"

- **Traditional reading (people of Israel)**: Most commentators take the speaker as the people of Israel personified, convicted by God's pleading and now asking — with a mixture of anxiety and self-righteousness — what sacrifices might appease God. The escalating offers (calves → thousands of rams → rivers of oil → firstborn child) show a pagan misunderstanding of what God actually requires. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: The question is asked "out of bitterness and resentment." Israel is essentially shouting at God from the witness stand: "You're unreasonable! Nothing will satisfy You!" Waltke is quoted: "Blinded to God's goodness and character, he reasons within his own depraved frame of reference. He need not change; God must change." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Some think the questions come from self-righteousness — as if the speakers had already done all that could be required. Others see a genuine (though misguided) acknowledgement of sin. The latter view is "most reasonable, and in accordance with Micah's manner." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/micah-6.html — summary from search)
- **Gill — Balak reading (distinctive)**: Gill argues this is NOT Israel speaking but *Balak king of Moab* addressing Balaam. He reasons: (1) The proposal of child sacrifice fits a pagan king, not repentant Israelites who knew God's abhorrence of it (Lev 18:21). (2) Balak had already offered sacrifices on high places (Num 22:41). (3) The "climax" of escalating offers culminates in child sacrifice — exactly what the king of Moab later did (2 Kings 3:27). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)
- **Ellicott**: Notes that Dean Stanley took vv. 6–7 as Balak's question and v. 8 as Balaam's answer — "a short dialogue preserved, not by the Mosaic historian, but by the Prophet Micah" — but Ellicott himself favours the view that it is the Jewish people personified. He also notes possible allusion to human sacrifice practices of Ahaz (to Molech) or Mesha king of Moab. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Precept Austin**: The people's focus is on external religious "works" to appease God. "Their real problem is that they did not come with hearts broken and contrite." God "always inspects the heart of the giver before He looks at the gift itself." Quotes Joel 2:13 ("rend your heart and not your garments") and Psalm 51:16–17. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)

---

### v. 8 — "He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?"

#### Traditional Reading

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: God cuts off Israel's angry ranting: "What I require is no mystery." The three requirements: (1) *Do justly* — act fairly toward others. (2) *Love mercy* — don't just show mercy, *love* to show it. (3) *Walk humbly with your God* — remember who God is and live accordingly. Quotes Spurgeon at length: true humility must come from the heart, not forced performance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Precept Austin**: This is God's answer — not ritual but moral obedience. Note the progression: two duties toward man (justice, mercy) and one toward God (humble walk). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)
- **JFB** (from search snippet): Justice and mercy are "preferred by God to sacrifices. For the latter being positive ordinances, are only means designed with a view to the former, which being moral duties are the ends, and of everlasting obligation (1Sa 15:22; Hos 6:6)." The three duties correspond to Christ's summary: "judgment, mercy, and faith" (Mt 23:23; Lk 11:42 — "the love of God"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/micah/6.htm)
- **Ellicott**: God "setteth more by mercy than by sacrifice," citing Ecclesiastes: "Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill** (reading this as Balaam's reply to Balak): This is Balaam telling Balak what the Lord requires of a *man* — not ritual sacrifices but moral righteousness, which is what the light of nature itself teaches (cf. Rom 2:14). To "do justly" as a king means to exercise public judgment and justice. To "love mercy" means to delight in showing mercy and liberality. To "walk humbly with thy God" means to behave with humility toward one's Creator — all duties knowable by natural revelation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

#### Baptist / Reformed Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God)

- **Piper** emphasises the wording: it does NOT say "love justice" or "do kindness." It says "**do** justice" and "**love** kindness/mercy." The distinction matters: "loving the idea of justice is cheap," but "doing justice" costs us personally. Conversely, it is easier to "do kind things" occasionally than to "love kindness" as a deep heart orientation. "The command to 'love kindness' pierces to the heart of things." Walking humbly with God is "to walk in repentance" — not in condemnation but in freedom. Piper ties this to the gospel: "what God requires of us in Micah 6:8, he purchases for us and accomplishes in us" through Christ. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lord-search-my-heart)
- **Piper** also applies this to Christian Hedonism: "the authentic heart of love loves kindness; it doesn't just do kindness." Loving acts are genuine to the degree they are not done begrudgingly but gladly. (https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/love-one-another-gladly)

#### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik on Enduring Word)

- Guzik's treatment is pastoral and application-oriented. The stress falls on how believers today "claim God's requirements are unclear or impossibly demanding" when they are not. He applies Spurgeon's sermon "Micah's Message for Today" with eight ways to walk humbly: when spiritually strong, when busy, in motives, in studying Scripture, under trials, in devotions, with fellow believers, and when dealing with sinners. The emphasis is on heart attitude over external performance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)

---

### v. 9 — "The voice of the LORD calls out to the city (and it is sound wisdom to fear Your name): 'Heed the rod and the One who ordained it.'"

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: "Hear the Rod!" has a double sense: the rod is both the corrective discipline of God *and* personified as the voice of God Himself. Israel felt the rod but did not "hear" it — they ignored what God was saying through affliction. Quotes C.S. Lewis: "God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks to us in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "Unto the city" = Jerusalem, "the metropolis of the wealth and sinfulness of Judah." The parenthetical "(and it is sound wisdom to fear Your name)" means: the wise person will regard God's name and see His hand in the visitations for sin. It functions like "whoso readeth, let him understand." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill**: Since the voice of the Lord by His prophet was disregarded, they are now called to hearken to "the voice of His rod" — the coming judgment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

---

### vv. 10–11 — "Can I forget any longer... the treasures of wickedness and the short ephah, which is accursed? Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?"

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: God is angry with Israel for cheating in business — "wicked scales," "deceitful weights." The sin was lying, stealing, and cheating one another for money. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "The scant measure" = literally "the hateful ephah of leanness" (less than it should be). Notes that the Jews were much addicted to falsifying weights and measures, citing Amos 8:5 ("making the ephah small and the shekel great"). Also cross-references the stringent Torah prohibitions in Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–14. "Can I be innocent with the deceitful balances?" — the implied answer is No. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)

---

### v. 12 — "For the wealthy of the city are full of violence, and its residents speak lies; their tongues are deceitful in their mouths."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: The sin went beyond cheating in commerce — the rich also used outright violence. Quotes Boice: "No society is ever entirely upright or godly... In times of moral breakdown this is inverted." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: The rich men practised "spoliation and fraud" without even the excuse of poverty. "They cannot open their mouth without speaking dangerous and destructive lies." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **StudyLight.org / verse-by-verse**: The rich men's houses and treasuries were "full of goods gotten by violent measures, by the oppression of the poor and needy." The poorer inhabitants used deceit and lies to cheat neighbours. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/6-12.html)

---

### v. 13 — "Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: God promises to make Israel "sick by striking" them — desolation because of their sins. This is the sentence passed by God as Judge after the case has been proven. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Pulpit Commentary** (via search): "I will make thee sick in smiting thee" — literally "have made the smiting thee sick," i.e., incurable (cf. Nahum 3:19), or "mortal blows." The perfect tense expresses the certainty of the future. Septuagint and Vulgate read: "I have begun [or will begin] to smite thee." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/micah-6.html)

---

### vv. 14–15 — "You will eat but not be satisfied... You will sow but not reap; you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil..."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: The judgment is one of "ironic deprivation." They will have food but no satisfaction; they will acquire things but not keep them; they will sow, tread olives, and make wine but never enjoy the fruit. This matches the curses of Deuteronomy 28 — covenant curses for covenant-breaking. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "Thy casting down" comes from an unused root meaning "to be void, empty" — hence hunger. "Thou shalt take hold" means to collect property for flight to save it, but in vain — it shall be captured. Treading olives (like wheat on the threshing floor) was essential; oil was "indispensable for personal comfort," and in Jotham's parable (Judges 9) the olive tree was regarded first in estimation, before even the vine and fig tree. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)

---

### v. 16 — "You have kept the statutes of Omri and all the practices of Ahab's house... Therefore I will make you a desolation..."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: Instead of walking in God's ways, Israel walked in the "sinful example of wicked kings." Quotes Clarke: "Omri, king of Israel, the father of Ahab, was one of the worst kings the Israelites ever had; and Ahab followed in his wicked father's steps. The statutes of those kings were the very grossest idolatry." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Ellicott**: This is especially damning because it is *Judah* being addressed (the southern kingdom), yet they adopted "the statutes of the house of Omri, the founder of the idolatrous dynasty of Ahab" — northern kingdom sins. "They reproduced the sins of the northern kingdom, and their conduct was aggravated by the advantages vouchsafed to them." Their reproach would be in proportion to the glory that belonged to them as God's people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
- **Gill**: The statutes of Omri and works of Ahab were observed "by them" — i.e., they walked in their counsels. The result: desolation, inhabitants a "hissing" (object of scorn), and bearing "the reproach of My people." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

## Denominational Distinctives on Key Verses

### On v. 8 — The "Three Requirements"

- **Reformed Baptist (Piper / Desiring God)**: Strong emphasis on the distinction between *doing* justice and *loving* mercy — the former is concrete action, the latter is heart affection. The gospel dimension: Christ fulfills what God requires. Walking humbly = lifelong repentance. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lord-search-my-heart)
- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik / Enduring Word)**: Emphasis on the practicality and clarity of God's requirements, with pastoral application through Spurgeon's eight-point sermon on walking humbly. Heart-level transformation is stressed: "Humility must be in the heart, and then it will come out spontaneously." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-6/)
- **Older Baptist (Gill)**: Reads v. 8 as Balaam's answer to Balak, grounded in *natural revelation* — what any man, even a pagan, should know. This reading is distinctive to Gill and a minority view. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)
- **Presbyterian (JFB)**: Emphasises the *priority of moral law over ceremonial law* — sacrifices are "positive ordinances" and temporary means; moral duties (justice, mercy, humility) are "the ends, and of everlasting obligation." Connects the three duties to Matthew 23:23 and James 1:27. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/micah/6.htm)
- **Evangelical (Precept Austin)**: Synthesises multiple traditions, focusing on the Hebrew word studies and the covenantal framework. The emphasis is that God "inspects the heart of the giver before He looks at the gift." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_6_commentary)

### On vv. 6–7 — Who Is Speaking?

- **Majority view (Israel)**: The people of Israel, convicted but resentful or misguided. (Guzik, Ellicott, Pulpit, Precept Austin)
- **Minority view (Balak)**: Balak king of Moab questioning Balaam. Held by Bishop Butler (noted in Ellicott), Dean Stanley, and John Gill. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/micah/6.htm)

### On v. 5 — "Righteousness of the LORD"

- **Traditional**: God's faithful, saving righteousness — His covenant faithfulness demonstrated in protecting Israel from Balaam's curse.
- **Ellicott**: The word more properly means "liberality, beneficence" — God's generous goodness to Israel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-6.html)
